lesson_title: The Folded Corner: Similarity Proves Pythagoras
hook_text: A ladder, a photograph, and one folded corner — that is the entire proof of the most famous theorem in mathematics.
clip_script: Prop a ladder against a wall and let the sun stretch its shadow. Climb a quarter of the ladder, and the rays mark a quarter of the shadow — parallel lines never play favourites. That is the proportionality theorem: a parallel cut shares out a triangle's sides in equal fractions. Now photograph a triangle and enlarge it: every angle survives, every side stretches by one factor. For triangles that reverses — match the angles and the enlargement factor must exist. Now the finale. Take a right-angled triangle and fold the right angle flat onto the longest side. The fold cuts the triangle into two smaller ones, and each is a photograph of the whole: a right angle plus a shared corner, and same shape is guaranteed. Same shape gives ratios; cross-multiply and each leg squared equals the hypotenuse times the piece of hypotenuse beneath it. Add the two: the pieces reassemble into the whole hypotenuse, and legs squared sum to hypotenuse squared. Pythagoras — proved by a ladder, a photograph, and one fold. And the crease keeps a bonus: fold squared equals piece times piece. Pieces of nine and sixteen? The fold is exactly twelve.
visual_style: A sunlit ladder throwing a measured shadow with glowing fraction marks, a triangle photograph zooming without turning, then a right triangle folding its corner onto the hypotenuse as squares bloom on each leg and merge over the hypotenuse.
mood: Ancient-mystery-meets-clean-logic, warm afternoon light, quietly triumphant.
pacing: Three unhurried picture beats, then an accelerating chain of ratios snapping into the final squared sum.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and own the proofs behind the most famous theorem in mathematics.
